sections.skill: Explain stock ownership and calculate gains, losses, and dividend income

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: What does owning a share of stock mean?

choices.text: Lending money to a company for a fixed interest rate
Depositing money in a company's bank account
Having a guaranteed right to a fixed yearly payment
Owning a small part of a company

questions.correct_answer: Owning a small part of a company
questions.intro: A stock (share) is a unit of ownership in a corporation. Shareholders can benefit if the company grows (the share price may rise) and may receive dividends, which are payments from profits. If the company does poorly, the share price can fall, even to zero.
questions.feedback: A share is partial ownership of a company.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jada buys 20 shares at $45 and sells them later at $52. Ignoring fees, what is her gain?
questions.intro: Gain or loss = (selling price − purchase price) × number of shares.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stock pays a yearly dividend of $1.80 per share. Omar owns 50 shares. How much dividend income does he receive in a year?
questions.intro: A dividend is a payment a company may make to shareholders, usually from profits, often quarterly. Dividends are not guaranteed; companies can raise, cut, or stop them.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stock price falls from $80 to $60. What is the percent change?
questions.intro: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A negative result is a decrease.

misconceptions.A: Divides by the new price, then uses a third

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Why do stock prices change?

choices.text: The government sets stock prices every morning
Buyers and sellers change what they are willing to pay
Prices rise by the same amount every day
Companies choose one price and never change it afterward

questions.correct_answer: Buyers and sellers change what they are willing to pay
questions.feedback: Prices move with supply and demand, which reflect news, company results, interest rates, and investor expectations.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Stock questions depend on separating owning a company (stock) from lending to it (bond) or depositing money (bank).

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which person is an OWNER of a company?

choices.text: Someone who lent it money through a bond
Someone who deposits money in a bank
Someone who holds its shares
Someone who buys its products

questions.intro: Shareholders own part of a company. Bondholders lend to it. Customers buy from it.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: If a company earns larger profits, what can happen to its shareholders?

choices.text: They must pay the company's taxes out of pocket
The share price may rise and dividends may grow
They lose their shares
Nothing ever changes for them

questions.correct_answer: The share price may rise and dividends may grow
questions.intro: Owners share in a company's success through price gains and dividends, and in its losses through price declines.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: If a company fails, what can happen to its stock?

choices.text: It can lose most or all of its value
It is repaid in full by the government
It turns into a bond that pays interest
Shareholders are paid before lenders

questions.correct_answer: It can lose most or all of its value
questions.feedback: Shareholders can lose their entire investment.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A company sends each shareholder $0.50 per share from its profits. What is this payment called?

choices.text: Interest
A capital gain
A premium
A dividend

questions.intro: Shareholders can earn money two ways: a capital gain when they sell shares for more than they paid, and a dividend when the company pays out part of its profits.
questions.feedback: A payment of profits to shareholders is a dividend.

misconceptions.B: Earned by selling for more than you paid

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A share bought for $30 is now worth $36. What is the gain per share?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Find a percent increase or a percent decrease
sections.relationship: Stock returns are percent changes in price.

ref_skill.name: Find a percent increase or a percent decrease

sections.skill: Interpret products of rational numbers in context
sections.relationship: Gains and losses multiply a per-share change (possibly negative) by the number of shares.

ref_skill.name: Interpret products of rational numbers in real-world situations

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A company reports much higher profits than investors expected. What is the most likely immediate effect on its stock price?

choices.text: It tends to rise
It tends to fall
It must stay the same by law
It drops to zero

questions.intro: Stock prices reflect expectations about a company's future profits. News that beats expectations often pushes prices up; disappointing news often pushes them down.
questions.feedback: Better-than-expected results usually raise demand for the stock.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stock's price rose 10% one day, though the company's business did not change. Which explanation fits best?

choices.text: The company doubled its size overnight that day
The SEC raised the price
Investor expectations or market mood shifted
Stock prices only change with profits

questions.correct_answer: Investor expectations or market mood shifted
questions.intro: Short-term price moves often reflect changing expectations, news, interest rates, and investor emotions, not just company results.
questions.feedback: Short-term moves often reflect sentiment and expectations.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: If interest rates rise, many stocks fall. Why might that happen?

choices.text: Stocks pay fixed interest that falls
Higher rates raise company profits right away
Interest rates and stocks are unrelated
Safer investments now pay more, so stocks look less attractive

questions.correct_answer: Safer investments now pay more, so stocks look less attractive
questions.intro: Higher interest rates make bonds and savings more attractive and raise borrowing costs for companies, which can lower stock prices.
questions.feedback: Competition from higher-yielding safe assets can lower stock prices.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A stock bought at $40 pays $2 in dividends over a year and ends at $44. What is the total return?
questions.intro: Total return includes price change plus dividends: (ending price − starting price + dividends) ÷ starting price × 100.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which statement about past stock performance is TRUE?

choices.text: A stock that rose last year will rise this year
It does not guarantee future results
Past returns set future prices by law
Only past performance matters

questions.correct_answer: It does not guarantee future results
questions.feedback: Past results are not a promise of future returns.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Picking individual stocks versus owning many

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Lia puts all $1,000 of her savings into one company's stock. The company has a major scandal, and the stock falls 70%. How much is her investment worth?
questions.intro: Owning a single company concentrates risk: problems at that one company affect all of your money.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Owning shares of 500 companies through a fund, with one company falling 70%, would affect the whole fund about how much (if that company were 0.2% of the fund)?

choices.text: About 70%
About 14%
About 0.70%
About 0.14%

questions.intro: In a diversified fund, a single company's loss is multiplied by its small share of the fund.

misconceptions.A: Applies one stock's loss to all

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Picking stocks that beat the overall market is hard, and stock-picking funds usually charge higher fees than index funds. What does this suggest for beginners building a core long-term holding?

choices.text: Low-cost diversified index funds are a reasonable core choice
Beginners should always pick individual stocks instead of funds
Stocks should be avoided entirely
Fees make no difference to results

questions.correct_answer: Low-cost diversified index funds are a reasonable core choice
questions.intro: Every dollar of fees comes out of the investor's return, and owning a few stocks concentrates risk. A broad index fund spreads money across many companies at low cost, though it still rises and falls with the market.
questions.feedback: Broad diversification at low cost is a sensible core holding for most beginners; it still carries market risk.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: What is a "ticker symbol"?

choices.text: The price of a stock
A government ID number
A short code that identifies a stock or fund on an exchange
A type of bond

questions.correct_answer: A short code that identifies a stock or fund on an exchange
questions.intro: Stocks and funds trade on exchanges under short codes called ticker symbols.
questions.feedback: Tickers are short identifiers used to look up and trade securities.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which source gives the official, detailed description of a company's business and risks?

choices.text: A social media post about the stock
Its filings with the SEC, such as the annual 10-K report
An ad for a trading app
A friend's tip

questions.correct_answer: Its filings with the SEC, such as the annual 10-K report
questions.intro: Public companies must file reports with the SEC, available free on the SEC's EDGAR database.
questions.feedback: SEC filings provide official information about businesses and their risks.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
